title: Briefing: France, Italy, Canada, Germany, Albania, India and Serbia
script: Good morning. It's Tuesday, November third, and this is the Unowned briefing: the stories that matter, checked and graded. It's read by a synthetic voice, and every fact comes from our published timelines.
Every item carries our grade. Confirmed means independent outlets agree. Reported means one source so far. Disputed means the accounts conflict. And alleged is one side's claim.
Here are the top stories.
France. Today: Education Minister says blockades deprive students' right to education as officials report dozens of schools disrupted.
Italy. Yesterday: Government cuts 350 teaching posts in Emilia-Romagna, UIL estimates 70-80 fewer in Bologna, FLC-CGIL calls strike.
Canada. Yesterday: Nine British Columbia First Nations announce court applications to quash Pacific Link designation, Ottawa offers 10% stake.
Germany. Yesterday: Education Minister Karin Prien deems youth protest concerns legitimate, promises dialogue; SPD urges education summit.
Albania. Yesterday: new developments in Albania's student protests.
India. On Sunday: Tens of thousands join opposition rally in New Delhi demanding Chief Election Commissioner resign.
Serbia. On Sunday: Thousands hold silent rain‑soaked march, lay 16 wreaths, observe 16 minutes silence, students demand punishment.
South Africa. No new developments since Friday, October thirtieth.
Now the details.

France. Today: France: officials said 48 of the country's 3,700 high schools and 51 of 184 higher-education institutions were disrupted on November third, while the USL student union put the number of blocked schools at about 500 and the Union Étudiante said over 50 campuses were blockaded. The USL denounced riot police deployed outside schools; Education Minister Édouard Geffray said on X that blockades deprive students of their right to an education. Our grade: disputed. The sides tell it differently, and both versions are on the story page. Coming up: Turnout and outcome of the unions' November fifth interprofessional strike and demonstration.

Italy. Yesterday, Monday, November second: Italy: la Repubblica reports the government's school budget plan would cut about 350 teaching posts in Emilia-Romagna, and the FLC-CGIL union says a strike is "the only choice". The UIL union estimates 70 to 80 fewer posts in Bologna province; the FLC-CGIL also criticises bonuses for private schools. We grade that reported: so far only la Repubblica has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation. Coming up: Turnout and outcome of the CGIL general strike called for November twentieth.

Canada. Yesterday, Monday, November second: Nine British Columbia First Nations announce Federal Court applications to quash the Pacific Link national-interest designation, saying Ottawa did not adequately consult them. Ottawa says it consulted more than 110 Indigenous communities and will offer a minimum 10 per cent ownership stake, The Globe and Mail and the Vancouver Sun report; Cold Lake First Nation filed the first challenge in October. Our grade: confirmed by independent reporting. Coming up: Whether binding Pathways carbon-storage agreements are signed by the November fifteenth target.

Germany. Yesterday, Monday, November second: Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien calls the concerns of the young people who marched in more than 30 cities on October thirty-first "legitimate and extremely relevant" and promises more dialogue, and SPD politicians call for a national education summit; these are proposals, not policy changes so far, The Local reports. We grade that reported: so far only The Local Germany has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation. Coming up: Gen Z regelt plans another countrywide protest on November fourteenth.

Albania. Yesterday, Monday, November second: Albania's jailed Tirana mayor, Erion Veliaj, accuses Prime Minister Edi Rama of orchestrating his October twenty-eighth prison transfer, which the government denies. Veliaj, held in pre-trial detention on corruption charges he denies, also said Justice Minister Toni Gogu demanded he give up control of the city, Tirana Times reports; the claims, relayed in part by his lawyer, are unverified. Our grade: disputed. The sides tell it differently, and both versions are on the story page.

India. On Sunday, November first: Tens of thousands join the INDIA opposition bloc's rally at New Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, led by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and backed by the Cockroach Janta Party, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign over a voter-list revision that removed more than 130 million names, AP and Reuters report. Health Minister J.P. Nadda calls it a "carefully orchestrated drama"; the Election Commission denies favouring any party and says wrongly removed voters can register again. We grade that confirmed: Al Jazeera and AP reported it independently. Coming up: The Special Executive Magistrate hearing for the CJP leaders summoned over the Jantar Mantar protest listed for the third week of November.

Serbia. On Sunday, November first: Thousands mark two years since the Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse that killed 16 people, with a silent march in the rain, 16 wreaths and 16 minutes of silence, AP and AFP report; students say they now want those responsible to be punished. Our grade: confirmed, with independent reporting from AP and Malay Mail. Also on Sunday: Prosecutors order the 48-hour detention of Marko Kričak, head of the criminal police, and another senior officer on suspicion of abuse of office linked to a murder investigation, AP reports. We grade that alleged: it's one side's claim, not independently confirmed. Coming up: Formation of the new government and the choice of prime minister.
Also on our watch, with no new developments in recent days.

South Africa. The latest report, from Friday, October thirtieth: A Durban court lets the anti-migrant group March and March keep demonstrating but only between 9am and 3pm, without weapons or face coverings and without damaging property, according to AFP copy carried by 24 News HD. Our grade: reported. It rests on one source, 24 News HD, and isn't yet confirmed by a second.
We'll bring you updates on those as soon as they become available.
Coming up in the days ahead. Wednesday, November fourth, South Africa: Local government elections on November fourth.
That's the Unowned briefing for Tuesday, November third. Full timelines, and every source, are at unowned news dot com. Thanks for listening.
